content_voiceover: This is the Shimoyama classification table that defines the four clinical subtypes of ATLL, and boards love asking you to distinguish them. All four subtypes require a positive anti-HTLV-1 antibody, that's the common denominator. The subtypes then split based on lymphocyte count, percentage of abnormal T cells, and organ involvement. Smoldering ATLL has a normal lymphocyte count below four times ten to the ninth per liter, at least five percent abnormal T lymphocytes, no lymphadenopathy, and no visceral organ involvement, essentially a skin-limited or minimal disease. Chronic ATLL has lymphocytosis of four or more, with abnormal lymphocytes present, but still no CNS, bone, ascites, pleural effusion, or GI involvement, distinguishing it from the more aggressive subtypes. Lymphoma-type ATLL is the nodal-predominant form, with a low circulating lymphocyte count, essentially no flower cells in blood, but histologically proven lymphadenopathy. Acute ATLL is the most aggressive and most common presentation, with variable lymphocyte counts, flower cells always present, and potential involvement of virtually any organ including CNS, bone, and GI tract. The key teaching point is that smoldering and chronic subtypes have relatively indolent courses and may only need observation or skin-directed therapy, while acute and lymphoma subtypes require systemic chemotherapy.
keypoints: Shimoyama classification: all subtypes require anti-HTLV-1 antibody positivity
Smoldering: normal lymphocyte count, >=5% abnormal cells, no organ involvement
Lymphoma type: nodal disease, low blood involvement, flower cells absent
Acute: most aggressive, flower cells present, can involve any organ
keypoint_voiceover: Four ATLL subtypes, one shared requirement: anti-HTLV-1 positivity. Smoldering and chronic are the indolent ones, with no CNS, bone, or GI involvement, and smoldering has no lymphadenopathy at all. Lymphoma type is nodal disease with few circulating cells and no flower cells. Acute type is the aggressive, most common form, with flower cells and potential involvement of any organ. Smoldering and chronic can often be observed; acute and lymphoma need systemic therapy.
